#102602. I Hunted Ducks and Geese During the Glory Days of Earthquake Lake

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2888 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

I Hunted Ducks and Geese During the Glory Days of Earthquake Lake

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it was a good day for waterfowl hunters.
  • I slid the overhead hatch back and stuck my head up and out of the blind.
  • In a recent development, the blind was one of the biggest I had ever seen, and it was also almost invisible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it was a good day for waterfowl hunters. Wisps of fog seeped out of the melting landscape, and the sky was so low and solid that the geese—if they came—would be close to the deck. And it was cold. Two days before, a savage cold wave had swept across Tennessee, plastering trees and highways with ice and freezing ponds thicker than anyone could remember. Ducks and geese had been sitting it out, but on this third day, the ice was melting, and they would fly.

I slid the overhead hatch back and stuck my head up and out of the blind. Earlier it had been too dark to see how we were situated. I found that we were in a soybean field of perhaps 300 acres, already plowed for the spring planting. There was sparse timber on all sides. To the south, the way hunters faced when standing in the blind, the timber was not so tall or thick, but there was the heavy undergrowth that grows at water’s edge. The lake is closer than I thought, I mentioned to myself. It’s only 100 yards or so away.

In a recent development, the blind was one of the biggest I had ever seen, and it was also almost invisible. From a duck’s overhead view, it no doubt looked like a rush-covered finger of land surrounded on three sides by timber, water, and waterfowl decoys—hundreds of them.

According to recent reports, thus oriented, I closed the camouflaged hatch and placed my feet near the gas heater. Sheer luxury! Being there almost made up for all those miserable days I have spent crouched in freezing mud holes. Perhaps a time or two before, in Texas and Louisiana, I’d been in more luxurious shooting stands, but they were small houses built on stilts above the water. This was a blind dug into the ground, lined with concrete, and covered with earth that had been planted with suitable cover. The blind’s eyes on the outside world were 12 sliding hatches.

Inside, the padded theater seats were as comfy as easychairs. Theater seats! I thought. Who in hell would have thought of putting theater seats in a duck blind? But it was perfect! The spring-loaded bottoms snapped up out of the way when you rose to shoot. That gave a man more foot and leg room and eliminated bruised shins if he turned around for backyard shots. I’m forever scraping my shins on the sharp-edged board benches found in most blinds.

It has been revealed that as the light increased, so did the yipping of the Canada geese rafted up on Lake Isom just beyond the brushy boundary. A few minutes before, the even din of honking had changed pitch when a raft of Canadas took wing. Moments later another flight heaved into the morning fog.

Our lookout Jerry Jones made no sign that geese were coming our way, but the atmosphere inside the blind was becoming so charged with excitement that you could almost touch it. Feet shuffled, experienced hunters quaked with anticipation, and hands rattled shotshells in jacket pockets to make sure fast reloads were ready. Overhead and close by, there was a whistle of teal. Jerry’s eyes followed their crossing flight, but he did not signal us to shoot, because he didn’t want to spoil our chances for the significant honkers that could be only minutes away.

Sources indicate that from the lake came another din of geese taking off, and Jerry pulled his head lower and tightened his grip on his Browning autoloading magnum. Then he crouched even lower, eyes level with his lookout hole, and said, “They’re ours boys. Get ready—now!”.

Industry observers note that shotgun barrels poked out of the blind, and there was ragged fire at eight or nine geese that were angling by to our left. The closest bird went limp in midair, but the one I fired at twice merely did the double wobble of a wise old goose that knows he’s being shot at.

Recent findings suggest that long ago I learned that in each flight of waterfowl there are one or two obvious birds. They are closer or bigger or out in front, and they tend to draw fire. When I’m sharing a blind with other hunters, I therefore pass up the obvious targets and go for a more obscure member of the flight. That bird is all mine, and I know for sure if I hit or miss. This time the obvious bird did draw most of the fire and was the only one to fall. Happily there was no chorus of “I got him!” that sometimes mars such events. These men, most of whom I’d met only that morning, were too experienced and too polite for that. Instead, each one claimed to have missed by several feet and that the goose must have been felled by the youngest member of the party, 15-year-old Charlie Lawrence.

It has been revealed that “I did?” he whooped in wide-eyed amazement. “And that means you’ll have to fetch it,” Charlie’s father almost managed to say before the young hunter was out of the blind and sprinting after the prize, his rubber boots going flub-flub and launching dollops of river-bottom mud from the Mississippi in all directions.

Whoever first noted that you can tell a lot about a man’s character by hunting with him really knew what he was talking about. Settling back into my posh seat, I knew I had learned a lot about my latest acquaintances already and had a feeling that we would all be good friends before the day ended.

According to recent reports, the only one of us who hadn’t pulled a trigger on the geese was Ralph McDonald, the well-known wildlife artist. His sliding hatch had stuck when the action started, so he had to sit out the first round. But Jerry Jones fixes that in a hurry by leaving the hatch open and covering the opening with a layer of cane that could easily be pushed aside. I liked that arrangement better than moving the hatch, so he fixed me up the same way. It gave me a better look at incoming birds.

In a recent development, in addition to Jerry, Ralph, and myself, our shooting party included H. Lea Lawrence, his teen-aged sons David and Charlie, country-music star Jim Ed Brown, plus Bill Morrison and Tom Callery. Lea, who lives in Nashville, is an outdoor writer whose name is familiar to readers of OUTDOOR LIFE. Morrison and Callery are field and legislative assistants to U.S. Senator William Brock of Tennessee. When I met Morrison and Callery that morning and learned of their political connections, I made a mental note to bend their ears about pending firearms legislation.

But there was no time for that now—ducks were coming, and Jerry was making seductive sounds on his substantial-barreled duck call. I couldn’t see the incomers from my angle, but it was easy enough to pinpoint their position by watching Jerry’s eyes. As they came closer, he crouched lower in the blind, and I knew they were within range even before he whisper-shouted, “Now!”.

About 10 spoonbills were winging low and fast from right to left in front of the blind. I swung my 12-gauge double, a Model 21 Winchester, through one of the trailers, but before I could press the trigger the bird’s head kicked back and he collapsed in midair. Then I was aware of three or four other ducks tumbling out of the formation, but my attention was concentrated on another spoonbill. I swung the barrels ahead by about two feet and pressed the trigger. The load of No. 4s folded the spoonbill so cleanly that there was no need to think about a follow-up shot, so I chased the barrels to the next closest bird and gave him the remaining round. It was a straightaway shot, and the range was rapidly increasing with each beat of his wings. For a moment it looked like a miss, but then the spoonbill did a turnover and went into a power dive before thumping hard on the semifrozen field. At 60 yards, perhaps more, it had been a lucky shot, but all eyes had been on me, and the welfare of my ego was at stake.

While David and Charlie fetched the downed waterfowl, I made the innocent mistake of asking Ralph if he had scored on the spoonbills. Though he is a leading wildlife artist whose paintings have twice been featured on the cover of the Ducks Unlimited magazine, he has a well-earned reputation as a hard-luck waterfowl hunter. On his goose hunts something always goes wrong, and he was still looking to shoot his first honker.

Jerry, who owns and operates Sunset Court and Dock on Reelfoot Lake, is one of those old-fashioned guides who believes that a day not spent hunting or fishing is a day wasted. Just to make sure that he and his customers get in plenty of both, his fees for a guided goose-and-duck hunt—including lodging, a heated blind, decoys, transport to the blind, plus some of the finest duck calling and yarn spinning you’re likely to hear anywhere—are no more than you’d expect to pay to spend the night in a rundown Upcoming York hotel.

While I was hunting the Reelfoot and Lake Isom area, the local waterfowl population was estimated at some 70,000 geese and about a quarter of a million ducks, mainly gadwalls and mallards.

Historic Reelfoot Lake is well known among waterfowlers and it is an easy day’s drive from many large Midwestern and Eastern cities. Lake Isom, however, remains distinctly undiscovered, even though it is only a few miles away (see map, page 89).

Sources indicate that hunting seasons run from December into January. The duck limit is based on the point system. Some ducks, such as pintails and spoonbills (shovelers), are rated at only 10 points each, so it is possible to bag 10 ducks plus two geese in a single day. That’s a lot of shooting.

It has been revealed that ralph was about halfway through a lengthy explanation of how he had failed to get off a single shot at the geese when Jerry shouted “Get down!” at the two young Lawrence brothers, who were still gathering ducks. Another flight of spoonbills had just cleared Isom’s boundary and were coming directly at us. Charlie had left his shotgun in the blind, but older and wiser David had his pump ready and neatly dropped a drake.

Recent findings suggest that the first half-hour had produced a goose and a half a dozen ducks—rich promise of a good day of shooting—but by midmorning the action tapered off to only an occasional shot at a passing duck. For some reason known only to themselves, the geese had decided to leave by the western side of the lake. We could hear their comings and goings, but none came within half a mile. Over a breakfast of ham and eggs cooked in a subterranean kitchen attached to the blind and complete with gas stove, we discussed the sagging action. Jerry allowed that we could move to a blind closer to the flyway the honkers had selected that day. Jerry owns or has access to 15 blinds.

After a quick scouting sortie, he asked for volunteers to try another blind situated where the honkers seemed to be heading, but he also told us the road was bad and we’d have to walk a ways. Jim Ed Brown, Lea Lawrence, and I volunteered, but not without some misgivings on my part.

Ralph McDonald elected to stay where he was, because, as he put it, he’d “… had a vision that the geese would soon come that way.”.

Even before we got to our newly introduced blind, there was no doubt that Jerry was right. While walking about a quarter of a mile through a sparse stand of scrub timber, we spotted three flights of geese skimming low over a field of winter wheat. They landed almost in the new blind.

Industry observers note that “Holy catfish!” remarked Jim Ed in the soft Southern accents that have made him a favorite of Grand Ole Opry fans. “All I need is two.”.

According to recent reports, just then six or eight more honkers slipped in low over the wheatfield, wings cupped to land. Before they touched down, the leader thought better of it, and they flared hard left, leveled off treetop high, and headed straight at us. We were almost through the scrub brush by then, and there wasn’t much cover, but we ducked into what concealment there was.

“Get ready,” Jerry whispered just an arm’s length to my left. Like me, he was half hidden in a honeysuckle bank. Just then Jim Ed and Lea opened up, and two honkers dropped at once. A third, hit hard, scaled overhead, and Jerry or me, or both of us, hit him at less than 30 yards and folded him cleanly.

In a recent development, the rest of the formation had swerved violently when Lea and Jim Ed started shooting, and they were out of range before I could come to bear with my second barrel. The geese were still reasonably close to Jim Ed, and with the last shot in his Model 12 Winchester pump, another Canada pitched down, wing feathers humming in the rush of the fall.

Sources indicate that “Friends,” drawled Jim Ed, “this is what I was brought up to call good goose hunting. I’ve got my limit, and we ain’t even in the blind.”.

The timing was perfect, because less than an hour later Jim Ed was scheduled to leave by charter plane to tape his popular “Nashville On The Road” TV show. So he and Jerry took the four honkers back to the truck while Lea and I went on to the blind. Jerry got back as rapidly as he could.

In a recent development, we had no more than settled ourselves when a flight of perhaps 20 geese came soaring up the field. Jerry called, and they began to circle. When we stood to fire, they flared sharply and momentarily gave us that near-motionless target goose hunters love. I shot at a bird on the far right end of the formation so there would be little chance that Lea and I would double on the same target. The Canada spun and fell without a flutter.

Meanwhile Lea was doing the same with a honker he had cut out of the flight.

Recent findings suggest that that evening we feasted on lake-country froglegs, catfish, hush puppies, and tart cole slaw. It had been a great day for everyone except Ralph McDonald.

“I was sure my hunch about those geese was a good one,” he lamented, pouring himself a stiff snort of Reelfoot tea, “but I never got a shot. My record is intact.”.

Read Next: I Gave Up My Duck Blind to Hunt Where the Mallards Actually Are.

It has been revealed that reelfoot Lake in far western Tennessee was formed by the New Madrid earthquakes of 1811-12. The catastrophe depressed some 50,000 acres that were later submerged by water from the Mississippi River. The surge was so great that the Mississippi is said to have flowed backward for a while. Due to siltation, plant succession, and drainage, Reelfoot Lake now covers about 18,000 acres.

A colorful legend accounts for the lake’s name. A Chickasaw chief suffered from a deformed or club foot and reeled when he walked. Chief Reelfoot could not persuade any of the Chickasaw maidens to become his wife, so he and his warriors kidnapped a Choctaw maiden named Starlight. Her father, who would not allow the marriage because of Reelfoot’s deformity, was so angered that he ordered his medicine men to bring down a terrible vengeance on Reelfoot and his people. That, the legend has it, was the cause of the earthquake.

Lake Isom, scene of the waterfowl hunt in this story, was isolated from the significant lake when a road was built around the southern end of the lake. A water-control structure and a ditch aided in draining the land that lies between the lakes today. The lake was given a name when the site was acquired for a waterfowl refuge from the Isom family.

Reelfoot’s excellent waterfowl habitat made it one of the most famous hunting areas on the Mississippi Flyway. The open-water portions attracted a variety of diving ducks, particularly canvasbacks. Mallards were most abundant and most popular among gunners. Eventually, however, the canvasbacks almost disappeared, and restrictive limits were imposed on mallard shooting. In the late 1960’s, with a one-mallard limit, Reelfoot had an all-time low in hunter usage.

Sources indicate that as the mallards and some other ducks increased in numbers after the low, and limits were increased, the popularity of Reelfoot Lake among gunners increased somewhat, but it is taking a while for hunters to realize that it’s the same hotspot. Reelfoot is as good today as it ever was, and Lake Isom is just as good. Neither Reelfoot nor Isom is managed by the state, but public hunting is permitted at Reelfoot. At Lake Isom the hunting is on private land.

Latest Update: 7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred.
  • Recent findings suggest that despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried.
  • Being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no plans for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred. They bore witness to her exceptional first 60 miles, during which she took the lead in under-course-record pace, all the way through to her gritting out the remaining 40 miles to a ninth-place finish. They spoke with Linden after the race to find out what she learned—and why she’s already angling to come back.

Recent findings suggest that despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried. I had followed her for the final half mile, camera rolling as her leg visibly seized up, likely from cramping. She had run 60 miles at course record pace, but still had forty to go—a long way without a fully functioning lower half. Linden sat on a chair and talked through the situation with her crew. A shoe switch, a lot more electrolytes, and roll the dice. Before I get into how the rest of her race played out, let me back up.

Being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no plans for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job. This is exactly what my business partner Nick and I did after getting the call to document Des Linden’s first 100-mile race at the Javelina Jundred on October 31.

Recent findings suggest that after landing in Salt Lake City, we picked up a camper van from Roadsurfer, threw our bags in the back, and headed south on I-15. A quick stop in Moab for a 50K race of our own was followed by four days evading floods and trying to figure out which desert roads were impassable after the recent downpours—which turned out to be pretty good foretelling for the race itself.

On the three previous occasions we’ve attended this event, it has been a delightful closing chapter to the season; Javelina has served as a sort of reward for making it to the end of our race coverage for the year, where the burden of logistics is removed from the job of filming. Instead of chasing athletes across the dirt roads of the Sierra Nevada at the Western States 100 or around a heavily glaciated massif at UTMB, the athletes at Javelina run in circles back to you. Five circles, to be exact. Adding to the enjoyment factor, Javelina is typically a giant Halloween party with racers and spectators dressed in costume under the warm desert sun.

However, this year was a little different. Deluge after deluge in the 24 hours leading up to the race saturated the race course. The sky relented just before the gun went off, but by the time the race had ended, over two more inches of precipitation had fallen. Not exactly what you expect for an event in the arid Sonoran Desert outside Phoenix, Arizona, but that’s why we love ultrarunning.

Recent findings suggest that we did our best to keep the cameras dry and our bodies warm as we followed Linden on her third ultra—well, fourth, if you count the road 50K world record. Despite a stunning road running resume, Linden was quick to point out that she’s still a newbie at trails and ultras but is excited to keep learning. Javelina’s first three laps were nearly perfect. But soon after her body shut down it was a struggle to make it to the finish line. At one point she had to stop for almost an hour, sitting and stretching until her legs finally relaxed and let her move again. And move again she did: Linden finished her first 100-miler as the ninth woman in 16:58:01, about three hours off winner Heather Jackson. We sat down with her the day after the race to learn her biggest lessons from the process.

Recent findings suggest that linden’s biggest takeaway from Javelina is to treat 100-milers, no matter the course, weather, or circumstances, with a ton of humility. Because they ask so much of your mind and body and are a completely unique style of racing, you can’t race a 100-miler like any other distance. “Just like when I started marathons,” Linden remarked, “I learned that if you’re cavalier with how you race it, you’ll pay the price at some point.”.

According to recent reports, linden was patient on her first 20-mile lap, sitting a few minutes back from the leaders. Feeling good, she picked up the pace on the next two laps, picking off all of the ladies in front of her to take the lead around the halfway mark. By the time she made it to the end of the third loop at mile 60, she had a six-minute gap on second—but her legs were starting to cramp.

Survival rapidly became the goal of lap four and the best way to do that was by listening to her pacer, Magda Boulet. Thankfully, there is no one on planet Earth better suited for the job. Boulet, a fellow U.S. Olympian in the marathon, is also a Western States winner and president of GU Energy Labs. She helped coax Linden forward, made sure she kept fueling, and stuck with her through all the ups and downs.

It has been revealed that one of Linden’s biggest challenges in the transition from road to trails and marathons to ultras is how much she needs to consume during a race—and how hard it is to catch up if she falls behind. At Javelina, Linden took most of her calories and carbs with fluids, drinking three half-liter (500 mL) bottles each lap. This fueling blueprint was developed for the typical heat of Javelina, but still worked well, as daytime temps almost hit 80 degrees Fahrenheit with 100% humidity.

Unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to keep her lower body from cramping around mile 60, which forced her to stop and stretch many times on the fourth lap. That setback resulted in her giving up the lead and ultimately the chance to win the race. “The fueling game has changed the sport,” Linden noted. “You see it on the roads, but especially here. It’s something I will keep working on, probably forever.”.

Assuming Javelina would be hot and dry like just about every other year, Linden packed for those conditions, putting her focus on cooling strategies and nutrition for the heat. She expected hardpack trails and excruciatingly hot sun, but the weather gods had other plans. Heavy rain required Linden and her crew to scramble to find key pieces of gear, including a raincoat. And because lap four took much longer than expected, Linden ran the last couple miles of it after the sun set, sans headlamp.

Industry observers note that next time she’ll prepare for worst-case scenarios, but will also understand when to pull the plug. “You need to know when to be tough and when it’s enough,” Linden remarked. “If I had to do another lap, I would have been on the edge of hypothermia and the trails were so, so slippery. There is nothing wrong with saving it for another day, but also great value in staying tough.”.

Sources indicate that pacing strategy is different at every ultra, but there are some broad themes that apply to the majority of runners and racers, especially for someone with Linden’s ability to close in the back half if she’s feeling good. Surprisingly, this is similar to how she used to strategize for marathons. The first third should feel easy, the middle third is about keeping the pace steady, and the final third is when the racing begins. “The first three or even three-and-a-half laps are transportation,”  Linden said, “the final lap or two is about racing.”.

In a recent development, when things got hard for Linden on the final two laps, she leaned into her crew to get to the finish. After a lap with Boulet, Linden picked up her husband Ryan as a pacer. He’s one of the most positive and energetic people you’ll ever meet, and his positivity and drive—paired with a little patience—helped get her through heavy rain and strong winds in the last 20 miles.

Recent findings suggest that her main support at Javelina HQ was Charlie Lawrence, the 100K world record holder and good friend. “A crew that knows you well, knows the sport well, and knows the emotional ups and downs of 100 miles is a real difference maker,” Linden said. “I was excited to be around everyone all week, so it was good energy going into the race, which is key.”.

It has been revealed that while Linden isn’t sure what the future holds or what her race calendar will look like next year, she walked away from the race with a surprising feeling. “I 100% want to come back to Javelina, it feels like unfinished business,” Linden said. “I didn’t think it would be this clear, but I know I can do so much better here.”.

A Bear to Be Thankful For: I Hunted a Record Black Bear on Thanksgiving Day

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 1966 deer season on the Keweenaw Peninsula, northern Michigan’s Copper Country, opened on November 12 and was due to close on the 27th, the Sunday after Thanksgiving.
  • It has been revealed that up to Thanksgiving day, our whole family had no luck.
  • The only family success scored was by my dad’s uncle, Bill Anderson, from Detroit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 1966 deer season on the Keweenaw Peninsula, northern Michigan’s Copper Country, opened on November 12 and was due to close on the 27th, the Sunday after Thanksgiving.

It has been revealed that up to Thanksgiving day, our whole family had no luck. My dad, my brother Bruce, and I had hunted hard and had seen deer almost every day, but nothing that we wanted to shoot. Even my mom, who goes along with us on our deer hunts but makes no pretense of hunting hard, had seen deer but had no shooting.

The only family success scored was by my dad’s uncle, Bill Anderson, from Detroit. He drove the 550 miles north to hunt with us, and went home with a good buck.

Industry observers note that I had special reasons for feeling disappointed about drawing a blank. I was born and grew up in the Copper Country. I’m now 24, and I’ve hunted deer since I was 14. That year my great-uncle Bill sold me his old rifle, a .32 Special Winchester Model 94. That old gun had killed a lot of deer and a few bears before I got it, and it went right on being lucky for me.

From that fall of 1956 until 1965, I killed a deer with it every year. Then circumstances compelled me to miss the 1965 season. I went into the Navy Reserve three years ago, and was called to active duty in the spring of 1965. When November of 1966 rolled around, I arranged for a leave to coincide with the deer season in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, and so I was back again, hunting the woods and swamps where I had been lucky ever since I was a kid, but not doing so well for a change.

It has been revealed that to make matters worse, I had to leave for the naval base at Norfolk, Virginia on  Saturday morning, November 26. I knew, when we left home right after breakfast on Thanksgiving day, that I had just that day and the next in which to kill a deer, or I’d wind up skunked for the first time in my life.

Sources indicate that we’re a Finnish family, all hunters and fishermen. My dad, Ernest Haataja, runs a refrigeration business in the village of Ahmeek, about 20 miles up the Keweenaw Peninsula from Houghton, the biggest city in the Copper Country. The peninsula is wild and rugged, and there are not too many roads. It’s a pretty fair game area, with deer, bears, coyotes, and bobcats.

Recent findings suggest that the Keweenaw juts northeast into Lake Superior like a rough and rocky finger, 50 miles long and 15 to 20 wide. In the small bays along the eastern shore, sheltered from the high winds and pounding seas of the great lake, there is excellent fishing, mostly for lake trout. The whole Haataja family loves to hunt and fish.

My brother Bruce is two years older than I am. He’s married, has four youngsters, works at a local mine, and does some beaver trapping as a sideline. We have three sisters: Vicki, 18; Carolyn, 10; and Mary Beth, 6. Pop, mom, and sister Mary Beth with the bear in Ahmeek, Mich.

According to recent reports, one of our favorite summer vacations for years has been to charter a small commercial fishing boat for a week or so and make the 50-mile trip on Lake Superior to Isle Royale National Park, the big, roadless island that lies 20 miles south of the Canadian shore. The fishing for lake trout there is as good as any we know about, and the sea lampreys have made lighter inroads than they have along the south shore of Superior. We have even seen lakers rising for flies in July and August around Gull Rocks, a few miles off the main island.

There is great pike fishing in some of the 30-odd inland lakes on Isle Royale, too, but we don’t care too much for pike and don’t often go after them. We live aboard our chartered boat, cooking our meals, sleeping on cots, and moving around as we choose. Isle Royale is 50 miles long, and there are plenty of sheltered harbors to anchor in. We hike, explore, and fish, and everybody has a fine time.

Bruce and I have had some other very good fishing trips together, too, including one to Lake Nipigon a few years ago that was a real adventure.

Recent findings suggest that the bear didn’t move a muscle. He just kept his eyes riveted on me as though trying to figure out what I was. Or maybe he knew, and tried to stare me down. Except for his head and round ears, he looked like a low-slung black bull, and he was so big he stunned me.

The family also has a cottage on Little Traverse Bay, about 15 miles from home, that we use for fishing headquarters in the summer and hunting in the fall. And from the time Rabbit Bay, nearby, freezes over until it breaks up in the spring, dad spends a fair share of his time fishing through the ice for lake trout. Fishermen are still catching trout out there with live lampreys attached to them, but some heavy stocking has been done, and the fishing continues to be fair.

Sources indicate that until I left home to go into the service, I never missed a chance to go along on those winter trips, and Bruce still goes as often as he can. Dad has built a set of light runners for a small boat, and if a hard wind is blowing offshore and there is danger that the ice may break loose and drift out into the open water of Keweenaw Bay, they take that outfit along. It’s so light that one or two men, going onto the ice on foot the way we do, can drag it easily. In an emergency, the runners can be taken off rapidly, and the boat is ready for use in the water.

I’m telling all this to help you understand how I felt about getting shut out on that 1966 deer hunt. I didn’t have any very good alibi, either. The weather was cold and clear, and hunting conditions were not bad although we had only a little snow-hardly enough for tracking_ The Keweenaw Peninsula sometimes gets as much as 20 feet of snow before winter is over. We had 234 inches by the end of March this year. But I had killed deer on bare ground plenty of times before, and thought I should be able to do it again.

Deer, however, are not so plentiful there as they were a few years ago. Many local people blame it on the opening of doe seasons, under special permit, by the Michigan conservation department. Whether or not that is the reason, we don’t see nearly so many deer as we used to, and we don’t see horns so often. But I knew that if I had to go back to Norfolk without filling my license, all that would be pretty cold comfort.

Sources indicate that thanksgiving morning dawned clear and cold with hardly any wind. The leaves would be dry and noisy underfoot, but it promised to be a fairly good day for hunting. We had been putting in most of our time in an area around Mud Lake, not too far from our cottage, but that morning we decided to try another location. We planned to drive out beyond Fort Wilkins State Park almost to the end of the peninsula. That’s as far north as you can go without getting your feet wet in Lake Superior.

Industry observers note that bruce drove our four-wheel-drive vehicle, and I rode up front with him. Dad and mom were in the back seat. Mom had packed lunch for the four of us. We’d stay in the woods until night. We usually start our deer hunting before daylight and hunt until dark.

Industry observers note that beyond Fort Wilkins we took a muddy logging road and then turned back toward Hoar Lake. A second logging road took us into remote, wild country miles from anywhere and near enough to the Superior beach so that we could faintly hear the noise of surf. We knew the place was a good area for deer, and even on Thanksgiving Day, there wasn’t much chance other hunters would find their way so far into back country.

On foot, we skirted a thick cedar swamp that lay between us and Superior, and we split up. Mom stayed behind. She found a spot where she could keep an eye on a runway along the edge of the swamp and revealed that she thought she’d have as much chance of killing a deer there as anyplace.

Knowing her habits, we suspected that she’d watch the runway for an hour or so, work around the end of the swamp, hike down to the beach, and look for agates. That was about what she did, too, but the swamp proved too much for her and for once she turned back and joined us for lunch without sighting Lake Superior.

Bruce and dad headed down into the swamp. I turned to the right, into massive, fairly open hardwood timber. There were high ridges running all through it with quite a lot of oak on the slopes. That meant acorns, and they are likely to mean deer.

The day had stayed bright and crisp. The ground was bare, and the leaves were really noisy underfoot, so I moved slowly, walking a few steps and then stopping to look in all directions. stepped carefully from one tree to another, trying to be as quiet as a cat and hoping I’d see a deer before me.

I found a little deer sign, but not so much as I had expected, and I was beginning to wonder whether I had picked the right place, after all. Then I cam over a rise, and a strange bare spot just ahead caught my eyes.

All around me in the timber, dead leaves lay in a thick carpet, but in front of me was a bare patch some 75 feet square. ln all the time I had spent in the woods I had never seen anything like that, and I stood there looking it over carefully, trying to puzzle it out. It seemed as though a huge vacuum cleaner had been at work.

Then, on the downhill side of the bare place, I saw a major mound of heaped-up leaves, and squatting in them was a black bear bigger than any I had ever expected to see. He saw me in the same instant, and we stood and stared at each other.

Read Next: Revolver Versus Semi-Auto: Which Is Best for Bear Defense?

Industry observers note that my eyes must have bugged all the way out of my head. The bear was less than 75 feet from me in open timber, not hidden by anything except his own leaf pile, and that fell far short of concealing him. Why I hadn’t seen him in the first instant after I came over the rise, I still don’t know, but I guess I just wasn’t looking for a bear. It was that bald spot, raked clear of leaves, that caught my attention and held it those first few seconds.

It has been revealed that the bear didn’t move a muscle. He just kept his eyes riveted on me as though trying to figure out what I was. Or maybe he knew, and tried to stare me down. Except for his head and round ears, he looked like a low-slung black bull, and he was so significant he stunned me.

For a moment I didn’t know whether to shoot or try to sneak away, but I made up my mind on that score in a hurry. I had seen bears in the woods once or twice during previous hunting seasons, but nothing like this one. I had never expected to have such luck, and I wasn’t going to pass it up.

Recent findings suggest that I don’t know how long we looked at each other. It was probably only 10 or 15 seconds, but it seemed like a full minute. I’ll say one thing: I didn’t get buck fever.

Sources indicate that I didn’t move a muscle either, until I raised my gun. The old rifle was not scoped, but at that short range, I didn’t need a scope. I brought my rifle up slowly and took careful aim. The bear standing partly sideways to me, I clouted him just below his left ear. The 170-grain softpoint knocked him as flat as a flapjack. He didn’t kick much, but he was an awful lot of bear, and he looked even bigger lying on the ground than when he was on his feet. So I walked close to him and put another shot into his shoulder to make sure.

Then I started looking things over. The bear had raked all the leaves downhill into one big pile, and only eight feet farther down the slope, I found a hole dug under a big cedar windfall. It was about four feet across and three feet deep and seemed freshly dug. If it had been used before, he had enlarged it and cleaned it out. Sand and gravel had been thrown in every direction.

Industry observers note that without much question, the bear had intended to use the pile of leaves for his winter bed. If I hadn’t come along, he probably would have dragged enough of them into the hole to line it before crawling in, raking the rest over himself, and curling up until spring. He would have had dry, snug quarters. The slope of the hill provided good drainage, and the windfall would have kept the worst of the snow off him. The leaves he had gathered would have been enough to cover three or four bears.

Sources indicate that he was a lot too big for me to dress without help, so I headed back to the car. Dad and Bruce were there when I arrived, and mom came along a little later. They had heard my two shots, and their first question was whether I had killed a deer. I stated no, and tried to string them along, but I guess my excitement must have shown.

“Well,” Bruce stated right away, “maybe you didn’t get your buck, but from the way you look you sure got something. What was it?”.

In a recent development, “It was a bear,” I blurted. “It’s the biggest bear I’ve ever seen. It’s so darned massive it looks like a grizzly!”.

“Did you kill it?” dad demanded.

“Deader than a salt herring,” I assured him.

Industry observers note that we hurried through chow, and then started back to the bear. When we got there, it was all the three of us could do to roll him over for dressing.

Sources indicate that as we worked, we debated whether we could drag him out to the nearest logging road. It didn’t seem very likely, for we had almost three miles to go on bare ground. It was plain that this bear was a huge thing for three men to handle, but we agreed to try.

Industry observers note that that turned out to be a big joke. We took hold of his head and forefeet, but we found that by tugging and grunting for all we were worth we could move him only a few inches at a time. We couldn’t have dragged him out of the woods in a month of Sundays.

I hated to leave him, but it was getting late in the afternoon, and there was no choice. We were sure no animal would molest him, and the area was remote enough so that there was very little chance other hunters would find him. Even if they did, he was so massive that nobody would make off with him. We hiked out to the car, laying intends to retrieve my bear in the morning.

In a recent development, we did some phoning that night and early the next day and learned that a logging outfit, the Kilpela Brothers from the town of Mohawk, was operating not far from where I had killed the bear. We contacted them, and to our great relief they said they’d hitch a dray behind one of their tractors and go in with us and bring him out. It was after dark before the job was done.

According to recent reports, I had taken a fine trophy. My bear was not only a record-setter for size, but also he had a thick, shiny, black pelt in perfect condition. There wasn’t a rubbed spot or blemish on it anywhere. It made as beautiful a rug as any hunter ever took. There wasn’t even one claw missing from the feet. That’s probably because there is no bear trapping in Michigan anymore. If there had been traps in the woods, he would almost certainly have blundered into one during his long life.

According to recent reports, we took him to Rinne’s Fuel Company in Ahmeek and weighed him on certified scales there in the presence of witnesses. We were all a little surprised at what the scales revealed. I had killed a black bear that weighed 570 pounds field dressed, the heaviest ever recorded in Michigan. He was 15 pounds over the previous state record holder. That one was shot in the 1950’s near Newberry farther east on the Upper Peninsula by Dean Loveless, a bowhunter from the downstate city of Hamtramck.

Michigan game men estimated that my bear had weighed not less than 650 pounds alive. His dressed weight was 82 pounds below that of the giant black killed in Wisconsin in 1963 by Otto Hedbany of suburban Milwaukee. That one dressed 652, and its live weight must have been around 725. Hedbany’s bear was described in “Biggest Black Ever Killed,” OUTDOOR LIFE, May 1964.

In a recent development, although I shot mine in the head, I did not damage the skull. My shot went in at the butt of an ear, and the bullet from the .32 Special opened up enough to kill him in his tracks. But it lodged somewhere in the brain cavity and did not come out. As a result, the skull was intact for measuring. I intend to enter it in the current Boone and Crockett Club competition, and the state game men tell me there is very little doubt that it will go into the record book, maybe not too far from the top. The Hedbany bear, by the way, was not eligible for entry, because the skull was shattered when it was killed.

Sources indicate that A photographer for the Houghton Mining Gazette came to Ahmeek that night, Friday, and took a picture of me with my bear. That was the only one I got of myself with the bear. It was too dark that night for us to use our camera, and I boarded a plane to go back to Norfolk early Saturday, so there was no time to think about more pictures. There were plenty taken after I left, but I wasn’t in them. That’s not too unusual for me. I’m the one in our family who takes the pictures most of the time, so I don’t appear in many.

I’ve promised myself one thing: If I should ever take another bear as good as that one, I’ll get some color pictures of myself with it, just to remind myself of my luck.

Read Next: The Best Bear Cartridges.

After we had gotten my bear into town and had weighed him, I had a chance to think the whole thing over. I couldn’t help feeling almost sorry I had shot him, but if I were doing it over again, I’d do the same thing. He was too much trophy to pass up. and I’m sure I’ll never in my life see another bear like him. Yet I did realize how long he had lived there in that wild country. He wasn’t doing any harm, and it seemed almost too bad that I came along that Thanksgiving morning when he was making his winter bed. He was my first bear, and much as I like hunting, if he should also turn out to be my last, I don’t believe I’d be disappointed.

On the other hand, shooting him was the most exciting thing that ever happened to me. I went back to the naval base without getting a deer, but I didn’t mind. That bear was all the Thanksgiving present any hunter could ask for.

According to recent reports, this story, “Bear to Be Thankful For,” appeared in the Sept. 1967 issue of Outdoor Life. The current Michigan state-record black bear, according to Boone and Crockett Club, is bear whose skull measured 22 11/16 inches and was killed in Newaygo County in 2009 by Donald R. Corrigan. Haataja’s bear is not listed in the B&C records.

Latest Update: Audrie Pelosi’s Couch Was “Always Open to Crash On”

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Michael Hall).

Audrie Pelosi found climbing after moving to Baraboo, Wisconsin. It wasn’t long before the quartzite cliffs of Devil’s Lake became a cornerstone of her life. She climbed there, worked there, and eventually became its steward as a guide with Apex Adventure Alliance (AAA), bringing upcoming climbers to the same arena in which she’d begun.

It has been revealed that “She was an exceptional climbing guide and human being,” Apex Adventure Alliance wrote in a statement to Outside. “She was a force in our community and at our guide service. We all will miss her dearly.”.

Originally from Duluth, Minnesota, Pelosi had long structured her life around her various passions: snowboarding, cycling, and, eventually, an all-encompassing love of climbing and the community around it. Her passion radiated outwards: she volunteered locally and, in 2026, ran for a Wisconsin Climbers Association board seat, hoping to become more involved in stewardship and community building. “I believe in showing up, doing the work, and listening to the community,” Pelosi wrote in her candidate statement.

According to recent reports, “With her friends and community, Audrie was so generous,” mentioned Garrett Hopkins, AAA’s owner. “That generosity flowed into her climbing, biking, and snowboarding too. When I was living on the road, I knew her couch was always open for a spot to crash if my van was being repaired. She spent countless hours with young climbers in an effort to elevate the safety of the next generation coming up.”.

In a recent development, pelosi met her husband, Jimmy “The Fox” Robinson, at a snowboard event at Welch Village, Minnesota, and in 2023 the two married atop Mount Bohemia (1,465ft) on Lake Superior. From then on, Pelosi had the nickname “Mrs. The Fox.” One of her friends, Anastasia Exterovich, set up a GoFundMe to raise money for Pelosi’s family in the wake of her passing. She called the pair the “raddest couple.”.

It has been revealed that “In my last conversation with Audrie, she joked about selling her handmade bike chain link earrings to anyone who wanted them for ‘free.99,’” Exterovich wrote. “It was such a simple statement made in passing, but it perfectly encapsulated who she was as a person. Even when she didn’t have much, she would give things away freely without hesitation, whether that was earrings, a smile, a laugh, a quick bike tune-up, or a belay.”.

Pelosi passed on May 30, 2026 working as a guide at  Devil’s Lake State Park, teaching a climbing course near the park’s East Bluff. During the course, Pelosi fell from the bluff and suffered fatal injuries. She is survived by her husband, her family, and the broader climbing community in Wisconsin.

Townsend Whelen’s Favorite Massive Game Hunting Cartridges

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4031 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Townsend Whelen, who was one of Outdoor Life’s first shooting editors and one of the founders of the legendary gun maker and outfitter Griffin & Howe, wrote extensively about significant game hunting from the early 1900s until his death in 1961. His articles on rifles, ballistics, cartridges, optics, and marksmanship have endured through the decades, thanks to his concise, informative prose that was based on years of practical experience as a hunter, competitive shooter, and career army officer.

He opined at length on the best cartridges for big game hunting, though he approached the topic with a characteristic open-mindedness. He was willing to consider and try new rounds as they became available, and loved to test out new equipment in the field and report on their results.

According to recent reports, I’ve unearthed Whelen’s favorite hunting cartridges by reading through his archived stories and books. One way to think of this list is as a snapshot of some key milestones in ballistic history, as well as an over-the-shoulder peek at the hunting rounds Whelen viewed as state of the art over his decades-long career. Many of his observations embody timeless wisdom and are still relevant today.

You’d think that among the cartridges he touted the .35 Whelen, which bears his name, would be included. After all, taking the .30/06 case—which was technologically advanced for the time—and necking it up for hard-hitting .358-caliber bullets was a winning combo.

For not much increased recoil the .35 Whelen launched bullets from 180- to 250-grains and rapidly gained a reputation as a solid big-game killer. (Most .35 Whelen loads feature one of four bullet weights: 180, 200, 225 and 250 grains).

Whelen mentioned the round in passing—notably to give credit to James Howe (of Griffin & Howe) for designing it—and briefly touched upon others’ accounts of it in the field. But if he ever hunted with it, or even shot it much, he didn’t document the experience. As far as I’ve been able to learn, he never messed with the round in any meaningful way—other than doing some hand loading for it—and its exposure to the general reading public was through other writers of the time like Elmer Keith, who hunted with it extensively and was a fan of the 250-grain spitzers.

READ NEXT: Two Rifles for the Ages, Chambered in .35 Whelen.

According to recent reports, this blind spot to his eponymous cartridge extended to the .400 and .375 Whelens, which Howe developed at the same time, though they never caught on the way the .35 did. If I had to guess, I would say that Whelen’s modesty, refined upbringing (he came from Philadelphia aristocracy), and soldierly sense of decorum precluded him from overtly praising the cartridge, rather than the existence of some undisclosed antipathy toward it. To ballyhoo something bearing his name would be unseemly.

Sources indicate that the list of cartridges Whelen recommended for big game evolved over the years. His career spanned an era of explosive growth in cartridge and bullet development as well as the adoption of such marvels as telescopic sights.

It has been revealed that for this reason, his earlier writings (from 1906 to the mid 1920s) prominently featured cartridges like the .30/40 Krag (aka the .30 Army), the .30/30 W.C.F. (aka .30/30 Win.), 7mm Mauser, .250 Savage, and their peers. Later on, he became a fan of rounds such as the .270 Win., .257 Roberts, and .348 Winchester. Throughout his long career, however, he never wavered in his praise for the .30/06 and the .375 H&H (with some qualifiers) when the topic of big-game hunting turned to cartridge selection.

Recent findings suggest that whelen’s career as an authority on hunting and shooting marched in lockstep with the creation of the .30/06 and its rise to prominence. He was intimately familiar with the round and could rattle off technical details in his sleep concerning its history, refinements, the pros and cons of the numerous available loads, and its qualities on the battlefield and for hunting.

He worked with the cartridge both in his capacity as a sportsman and as an army officer—particularly after World War I when he transferred from Infantry to Ordnance, eventually becoming the commanding officer at Frankfort Arsenal and the director of research and development at the Springfield Armory.

Sources indicate that he hunted extensively with the .30/06, killing all manner of significant game during his many adventures. One of his preferred projectiles was Western Cartridge Company’s 180-grain open point boat tail bullet, with which he killed a grizzly bear, three moose, two caribou, two bighorn sheep, four mountain goats, and six deer.

Sources indicate that he documented his experience with this bullet in particular because of occasional reports of 180-grain bullets failing on game. He wasn’t buying it.

It has been revealed that “There has never been even a suspicion of a failure on any of the game I have shot with it,” he wrote. “Many other sportsmen have had a similar experience.”.

Recent findings suggest that he found the bullet delivered good accuracy as well. “In my own rifle it was averaging about 2-inch groups at 100 and 4 inches at 200, and I got one moose killed clean at 325 yards and two goats killed likewise clean at 325 and 350 yards,” he said.

On bigger game, many hunters gravitated toward 220- and 225-grain bullets back then, and the relative killing power of those bullets when compared to the wimpy 180s was a hot topic of discussion.

Whelen gives the heavier bullets their due, in particular the 220-grain soft points: “This bullet has made a very enviable reputation for fine killing power on larger game, and particularly on moose and Alaskan brown bear.”.

But when it came to terminal ballistics, a topic he was better versed in than most, he didn’t go along with the accepted wisdom that bigger meant better.

“It is generally supposed that the 220- and 225-grain bullets are more reliable killers on our larger game than those of 180 grains. I am not so sure of this,” he said. “I would put them about on a par with the best of the 180-grain bullets up to 200 yards. Beyond that distance the trajectory of the 220 grain bullets becomes too curved to surely hit a deer or animals of that size.”.

In his opinion the effectiveness of those heavy bullets topped out around 225 yards, while the 180s and 172s could hit accurately and kill game to 350 yards.

If he sounded like he held strong opinions on the .30/06 that’s because he did. He never hesitated to discuss—and defend—its effectiveness on game, but he also didn’t hold back critiques either.

For instance, he took ammunition manufacturers to task in the 1930s for allowing the general quality of .30/06 ammo to slip. He had three “fine scope sighted rifles of Springfield, Winchester, and Remington makes” in his collection and gathered data that indicated accuracy had fallen off from an average of 1 ¾ to 2 inches at 100 yards to 3-inch groups, while at 200 yards ammo that used to print 3 ½- to 4-inch groups now couldn’t shoot better than 7 inches.

READ NEXT: .30/06 Cartridge Review.

He felt ammo makers were neglecting the round in favor of newer offerings that were in the limelight and used the power of his platform at Outdoor Life and other publications to chastise those companies.

“With such ammunition a fine .30/06 rifle is no longer a 350-yard rifle, but rather a 225-yard arm for sure hits,” he said.

The reason for his bluntness was that he hated the idea of the .30/06—which he said is “never a mistake”—not living up to its potential as our best all-around significant game cartridge.

Sources indicate that not many deer hunters today would list the .250 Savage among their top picks for whitetails—assuming they’re even aware of the cartridge’s existence. A lot of them would dismiss it as underpowered, though that would have come as a shock to Whelen. I guess whitetails have become more bulletproof since his day.

But when ballistic visionary Charles Newton created the .250-3000 in 1915 for the Savage 99 lever action, he gave American sportsmen their first high-power round capable of pushing a bullet at 3000 fps.

To be clear, Newton favored 100-grain bullets in the round with a muzzle velocity of 2800 fps, but Savage wanted to break the 3000-fps barrier and loaded it with 87-grainers which would do just that.

A lot of hunters jumped on the .250 Savage bandwagon and quickly demonstrated its worth in the woods.

“It has proved to be a very good deer cartridge,” Whelen wrote. Adding, “from hundreds of reports from the game fields it is quite clear that it gives a much larger percentage of instantaneous kills on deer with the first shot than does the .30/30 cartridge.”.

Industry observers note that whelen shot the .250 with 87- and 100-grain bullets, developing handloads for both. He favored the lighter bullet for small game, and the 100-grainers for varmints and deer.

READ NEXT: Best Deer Hunting Cartridges.

When he first recommended the .250 Savage for deer, the .257 Roberts hadn’t been developed yet. By his own admission in later years, he felt anything the Savage could do the Roberts could do better.

“I think that a well-informed rifleman would hardly choose this cartridge because the .257 Roberts cartridge slightly excels it in every respect,” he remarked.

I’m taking a bit of liberty with this one, as when Whelen wrote about mule deer earlier in his career he advocated the .30/30 W.C.F. as a minimum acceptable cartridge and, as he often did, defaulted to the .30/40 Krag with a 220-grain bullet as optimal. That said, he did throw in a qualifier that any cartridges for other Western game would serve well on muleys.

After the .270 Win. came on the scene, Whelen became a huge fan, calling it “one of the finest cartridges we have for American major game shooting—a very remarkable load.”.

He extolled the killing power and flat shooting characteristics of Winchester’s 130-grain spitzer bullet and described how a moose he shot with it “was killed more instantaneously than I have ever seen a moose killed before or since.”.

Industry observers note that his Winchester Model 54 was the most accurate big game rifle under 10 pounds he owned—capable of printing 10-shot groups at 100 yards measuring 1 7/8 inches, and 4-inch groups at 200. Relative to harder-kicking cartridges like the .30/06, the soft-shooting .270 lent itself to “fine practical accuracy.”.

As much as we link Jack O’Connor and the .270 Win., there’s little doubt as to Whelen’s perspective: “I think it is our best American big game cartridge in the hands of a rifleman who can avail himself of its flat trajectory and fine accuracy.”.

When Whelen joined the Army in the late 1890s prior to the Spanish American War, the .30/40 Krag (aka the .30 Army and .30 US) was the standard issue round. It didn’t serve in that role long. It was adopted in 1892, replacing the .45/70 and then was ousted by the .30/03 (which later became the .30/06) in 1903.

But like most cartridges employed by the military it became a hit with the sporting public, and as one of our first domestic smokeless powder rounds hunters took a shine to it. It shot a metal jacketed round nose 220-grain bullet at 2000 fps from a 30-inch barrel, which was hot stuff back then. In a carbine configuration with a 22-inch barrel, the velocity dropped to 1960 fps, which was still impressive for the time.

In 1899, a hunter killed the world-record Rocky Mountain elk with a .30/40 Krag, which cemented its reputation as good medicine for wapiti.

READ NEXT: Best Elk Hunting Cartridges.

Recent findings suggest that whelen liked the .30/40 Krag for elk, too. When he expressed this opinion in his book, American Major Game Shooting, he felt it was the minimum one should attempt to hunt elk with and made a point of emphasizing the use of the 220-grain bullet rather than some of the lighter projectiles available.

That remarked, in 1923 he gushed about the capabilities of the .30/40 Krag with a 180-grain open point bullet, declaring it “the most useful and all around successful cartridge ever made for the American sportsman.”.

This round is all but forgotten today, having been consigned to the ballistic graveyard in 1936 when Winchester ditched it, along with the Model 1895 rifle that it was chambered in.

But from 1903, when it was developed, through the Roaring 20s the .35 Winchester had a respectable run as a major-game round that fell in between the .30/30 and the .405 Winchester, both of which are still produced today.

It has been revealed that like the .30/30 and .405, the .35 W.C.F. is a rimmed bottle-neck cartridge that shoots soft-pointed lead bullets from lever actions. Launching a 249-grain lead cast bullet at 1,500 fps would be plenty potent for moose, which is why Whelen mentioned this cartridge in American Big Game Shooting.

READ NEXT: Best Moose Cartridges.

Of course, being a magnanimous sort, Whelen also lauded the .30/06, the .405, and later on cartridges like the .270 Win., as good options for moose hunters.

Nowhere does Whelen reveal his level-headed style of analysis more than when discussing hunting large bears. He loathed exaggeration as much as he loathed excessive recoil, so when discussing the best all-around bear cartridges he walks a fine line in terms of his recommendations.

On the one hand, he discusses how tales of the ferocity of grizzly bears are vastly overstated—but without minimizing their toughness. “Today there is little danger attending the hunting of the grizzly for a fairly good shot, equipped with a modern rifle of fair killing qualities,” he remarked. “However, a grizzly can carry away an awful amount of lead, and from the standpoint of obtaining the bear as well as for protection, a powerful rifle is desired.”.

What qualified as “powerful,” according to Whelen, were the .30/40 Krag, .30/06, .405 Winchester, .35 W.C.F., and the .375 H&H.

It has been revealed that he rightly noted that the .375 H&H was a cut above those other rounds. At one point he described a scenario where when hunting large coastal brown bears in thick cover around salmon streams carrying a stopping cartridge like the .375 H&H was the way to go.

But he also understood the limitations of the round in terms of practical accuracy for most hunters.

“The recoil is not severe to the thoroughly trained rifleman, but is rather heavy for the novice and the ordinary sportsman,” he noted. He goes on, “I find that in many cases sportsmen have selected a rifle for this cartridge because they have had failures with the .30/06 cartridge. In almost every case of this kind, if we analyze the seeming failures with the latter cartridge we find that they are due either to a lack of skill in marksmanship, or else the wrong type of .30/06 cartridge was chosen for the game in question. The .375 Magnum cartridge will not in any sense make up for any lack of skill in marksmanship.”.

READ NEXT: Best Bear Hunting Cartridges.

He continues to hammer home this point, saying that a typical sportsman will be ill served trying to overgun for any animal, and is better off shooting a milder round with an appropriate bullet.

“It is certain that if one is a poor or only ordinary shot, he will shoot much worse with a rifle taking the .375 Magnum cartridge than with one less heavily loaded, due to recoil.”.

That perspective is as valid today as it was more than 70 years ago.

This entry requires a bit of a caveat. First off, when Whelen first wrote about hunting black bears in American Significant Game Shooting, he didn’t offer a recommendation as to which cartridge to use. It is the only animal in that book that he declined to list one for.

Industry observers note that his reason for doing so was because he didn’t care to hunt them himself and wanted to see them protected by adequate game laws. At the time, bear hunting was largely unregulated and they were regarded as vermin. “The black bear is the only species of American game that I have not shot, and I never want to,” he said.

“The black bear is the most amusing, ludicrous, human, and understandable of our wild animals, and in captivity it makes a most interesting pet…. It is entirely harmless, except on rare occasions, and it should be protected by proper game laws and permitted to survive,” he wrote.

That said, the book, which he did in conjunction with the Western Cartridge Company, had a picture of the above-mentioned .35 Winchester Cartridge under the black bear entry, which was a good all-around significant-game woods cartridge.

The rise in popularity of the .35 Remington no doubt hastened the .35 Winchester’s demise. It was initially offered in Remington’s Model 8 autoloading rifles and was later chambered in Remington Model 14 and 141 pump actions and the Model 30 bolt gun. Marlin started chambering it in their lever-actions in 1953.

All this is to say that Whelen recognized the capabilities of the .35 Remington as an all-around option for deer, bear, and other animals.

Sources indicate that “It is a good cartridge of moderate power and range for use on all American big game. It kills very well at medium ranges, being in this respect much superior to cartridges of the .30/30 class,” he said.

Industry observers note that he felt the cartridge was a good match for the Remington Model 141 in particular. “Deer will be killed much more quickly and reliably than with the other cartridges adapted to this rifle, and (in the rifle it) is by no means out of the running for moose, elk, or large bear.”.

According to recent reports, among all the cartridges Whelen spent time with, the quarter-bore “Bob” was his all-time favorite. He was in touch with Ned Roberts during the development of the .257 Roberts in the mid-1920s and encouraged him to call it the “.25 Roberts” in light of the effort he put into creating the round, which is based on a necked-down 7×57 Mauser.

It has been revealed that “I think that no man has ever spent so much time in perfecting a cartridge as Mr. Roberts spent on this one,” Whelen wrote.

Whelen who was an avid varmint shooter and one of the driving forces behind the development of benchrest shooting, loved small, accurate cartridges so it is no wonder he took to the Roberts when it was introduced.

He favored 100-grain bullets for their flat shooting and hard-hitting capabilities on woodchucks out to 300 yards and on crows to 200 yards.

“I do not know of a finer long range varmint cartridge than this, particularly with hand loaded cartridges,” he stated.

Recent findings suggest that he didn’t feel it was limited to popping chucks, however. “It has been proved innumerable times that the full charged cartridges loaded with 100- and 117-grain bullets give excellent results on deer, and we therefore here have a most excellent all-around cartridge which a rifleman can use all year round for small game, varmints, and target, and then take into the massive woods after deer in the fall,” he said, adding that other than for moose and elk it was a good option for other game, including antelope.

Read Next: Best Antelope Cartridges.

Because of its light recoil, relatively soft report, excellent accuracy, and—for the time—wide bullet selection he said it would get the nod as the one cartridge he’d pick if could only shoot one.

“I consider it a very fine cartridge, and if I had of necessity to confine myself to one rifle only I would choose it in this caliber,” he remarked.

Whelen didn’t mince words when it came to hunting sheep and goats. He knew through first-hand experience how challenging those animals are, both in terms of the terrain that needed to be traversed to get to them and the difficult shots a hunter was often confronted with.

Sources indicate that “The hunting and stalking of them is so difficult that the head of a substantial ram killed by fair stalking is the most prized trophy that can fall to the rifle of the American hunter,” he said. “Often the stalk ends with the hunter quite a long distance from his game with no chance of getting closer unobserved…for this reason a rifle adapted to a cartridge of very high velocity and extreme accuracy at long ranges is most desirable.”.

The two cartridges he touted as most capable for this work were the “.30 caliber Model 1906” shooting a 180-grain “Open Point” and the 7mm Mauser shooting a 139-grain open point.

In his personal 7mm Mauser he was able to swap between 175-grain expanding bullets for large game and the 139s when it came time to go after deer, sheep, goats, antelope and varmints.

When zeroed with the 139s at 100 yards, the 175s shot to point of aim at 200 yards, giving him the confidence to swap ammo as needed on the fly.

But he warned his readers not to count on that trick working in their personal guns.

Recent findings suggest that “Sometimes such a combination can be worked out for certain rifles, and for some it cannot be accomplished. It is not so much a matter of cartridge, caliber, or make of rifle, as how the individual barrel vibrates with each load.”.

One thing that’s clear to me is that Whelen would have been a fan of the 6.5 Creedmoor. He loved mild, accurate, and effective cartridges, particularly when loaded with the proper bullets, and didn’t hesitate to employ them on major game.

It shouldn’t come as a shock then to see him sing the praises of the 6.5x54mm Mannlicher Schoenauer as a good choice for caribou.

Industry observers note that “Caribou are often found in open or partly open country, and the careful stalking necessary to bring them to bag, with attention to wind, sight, and hearing, make their pursuit a splendid sport,” he mentioned. “As they are often in localities where it is impossible to approach very closely, a rifle which is effective at long range is very desirable, usually one firing a military or semi-military type cartridge.”.

He claims that caribou deserve a cartridge along the lines of what one would use for elk and lists the .30/06, 7mm Mauser, and 6.5mm Mannlicher as examples—all of which were standard problem military rounds at the time.

Recent findings suggest that whelen’s eclectic and open-minded approach to cartridges was a defining characteristic of his. So narrowing down a list of his favorite rounds is a bit tricky.

On the one hand, in 1923 he called the .30/40 Krag the “most useful” and “successful cartridge ever made for the American sportsman” that “will kill with a single shot any game in America.” He supported that statement with anecdotes of his own success with the .30/40 Krag in the field, including a one-shot instant kill on an 18-foot crocodile. Fast forward 17 years to 1940 and he doesn’t even mention the round in his thick tome, The Hunting Rifle.

That was in part a function of the rapid pace of small arms and ammunition development at the time. Whelen’s job was to be on the cutting edge of all things ballistic, and he refused to stick with something out of a sense of nostalgia.

It has been revealed that that remarked, having read much of what Whelen wrote I’ve aimed to do him justice with the rounds I picked. All of the cartridges mentioned are ones he bestowed his imprimatur upon, though I will be curious to see what other fans of “Townie”—as he was called by his friends—think his favorites would have been.

Industry observers note that this is the gear we'd buy to get out more without spending more. (Photo: Colton Stiffler).

Atomic Hawx Prime 100 Ski Boots.

Industry observers note that overview: SKI’s editors curated 12 value-oriented picks for skiers who want to spend less while getting out more. The list includes Line Pandora 106 skis, Atomic Hawx Prime 100 ski boots, Flylow Firebird bibs, and Scott Shield goggles, plus money-saving accessories like a boot pack, soft cooler and rub-on wax.

According to recent reports, skiers aren’t all loaded vacationers willing to drop $20,000 on a weeklong ski vacay once a year. In fact, most aren’t. Most of us want to spend as little as possible while getting out as much as possible, so we sniff out the best deals on lodging and lift tickets whenever we can. The same applies to gear. You don’t necessarily want the cheapest of the cheap, but high-performing items that strike a solid balance and stick with you for seasons to come. If that’s you, read on. These are our top budget-friendly gear picks for value-minded skiers—plus some money-saving hacks to save you more on the hill this season. And if you’re looking for a place to take try out all your new gear, check out SKI’s Best Value Resorts of 2027.

It has been revealed that A playful and reliable wide all-mountain ski, the Line Pandora 106 has been one of our favorite skis for years—plus, it retails for $699 and is currently on sale for even less, making it a couple hundred dollars cheaper than similar freeride skis. With a 106-millimeter waist, it’s a perfectly reasonable companion for a surprise 10-inch storm while still holding a solid edge on groomers. A short 18-meter turn radius delivers a light and nimble feel that intermediate and advanced skiers can both enjoy.

An approachable yet capable all-mountain ski, the Atomic Bent Chetler 85 is perfect for cruising groomers, letting loose on side hits or progressing in the park. A short turn radius—16 meters at the 170 centimeter length—and a lightweight wood core make it easy to flick these planks around, whether you’re hitting the park or looking to arc some dad turns with the fam. The narrow 85 millimeter waist, while not ideal for a deep day out West, ensures easy edge-to-edge transitions—an ideal, playful everyday ski for East Coasters and on-piste skiers.

Intermediate-to-advanced ski boots are hard to find fresh for under $500, and the Atomic Hawx Prime 100 strikes an excellent balance of performance, durability and comfort—proving that you don’t need the stiffest boot on the shelf to enjoy a solid day on the hill. The 100 millimeter last and medium volume fit accommodate average-sized feet, and Atomic’s Prolite shell construction keeps weight low, lightening the shell with targeted areas of thicker plastic for stiffness and response. Available in men’s and women’s models.

The Smith Method is a classic helmet that protects your noggin without many bells and whistles, and we love it for its minimalist look—and minimalist price point. A lightweight Koroyd shell design stands up to impacts and wear and tear, with two vents in the front and four in the back to keep the air flowing on warmer days. The ear flaps are removable if that’s your jam, and it comes in tons of colorways. A little pricier, the Method is also available with MIPS technology.

While most brands’ prices for ski outerwear have skyrocketed, Truckee, California-based Flylow has somehow held on to approachable pricing for a lot of its gear, and we as skiers thank them for it. The Flylow Knight Jacket is a fully seam-sealed 3-layer waterproof shell, with spacious external pockets, a powder skirt to keep the elements out, and a storm hood to block the howling wind. Zippered underarm pockets dump heat on warm spring days, and the relaxed fit makes it easy to layer a puffy underneath.

Flylow’s Firebird Bibs have been a popular style for years now, and for good reason. It’s rare that you’ll find such a capable bib for under $400, much less one that’s chock-full of thoughtful features. Built with a 3-layer Intuitive waterproof membrane and a high-coverage design, these bibs are ready for deep storm days. Ample zippered pockets on the chest and thighs make it easy to stuff snacks or a sandwich, and side venting lets heat escape when you’re working hard for your turns.

It’s easy to spend $250 to $300 on ski goggles, but if all you’re looking for is comfort and a solid field of view, the sub-$100 Shield Goggles from Scott are an excellent value option. The cylindrical lens and semi-frameless design offer an impressive field of view, with an anti-fog treatment, comfortable 3-layer face foam and a wide strap that stays securely on your helmet. That’s a lot of goggle for the money.

Made for ski bums by ski bums, Flylow’s Ridge Gloves are a versatile tool for resort and backcountry skiing. Synthetic insulation and DWR-treated pigskin leather keep your hands dry and warm while storm riding, and the low-profile stretchy nylon cuff slides easily under a ski jacket for a minimalist feel. These aren’t the fanciest gloves in the world, but they sure can take a beating.

It has been revealed that as tempting as it can be to park right at the base of the gondola, one of the best ways to save money at a ski resort is skipping the primo parking. If you have to hop on a shuttle, it can be nicer on your feet to boot up once you get to the resort. Atomic’s Boot + Helmet Pack is a 35-liter backpack, ideal for hauling your gear to the base area if you end up parking miles away. Stashing boots, gloves, helmet, goggles and extra socks makes a short commute to the hill feel all the more civilized when you aren’t sweating up a storm fully kitted up an hour before you start skiing.

According to recent reports, resort lunches—while delicious—are one of the quickest ways to blow through a vacation budget. Packing a few sandwiches and snacks in a small cooler like this Mountainsmith Takeout 6L can save a family hundreds on lunches over the course of the season. It’s compact enough to stash under a bench or in a small locker at the base. And if a bowl of chili in the lodge is non-negotiable, at the very least you can stuff this cooler with a sixer of beer and save some cash at the bar.

In a recent development, tailgate après vibes are an easy way to cut down on costs at the resort, but it takes a little bundling up—and a lot of beer—to get your friends to want to stick around. Chaco’s Ramble Rugged Shoes are the perfect outside-ready slipper to slide your tired feet into at the end of a ski day. The cozy fleece lining is soft and warm, while a quilted water-resistant canvas upper provides solid protection for your feet while you post up next to a snowbank. The adjustable strap lets you snug up the fit, and rubber soles hold traction in icy parking lots.

It has been revealed that instead of dropping off your skis at the local shop for a quick wax, do your own basic maintenance and save a chunk of change. This brick of Swix F4 Glidewax is a universal rub-on wax that’s easy to stash in your boot bag for quick touch-ups when you need them. Sure, it’s no replacement for a full tune, but when temps are fluctuating and you just need that extra bit of glide, this rub-on wax will do the trick—and save you at least $50.

It has been revealed that saving money on a ski trip doesn’t mean cutting corners. Buy smart up front, then let a few small habits—a quick rub-on wax, a packed lunch, a tailgate après sesh—keep the little expenses from piling up. That leaves more of your budget for the part you came for: skiing.
